questiontext.text: In a hash table using separate chaining, what does each bucket (table slot) hold?

answer.text: A linked list (or similar structure) of all entries that hash to that slot

feedback.text: Correct — colliding keys are stored together in the chain at that bucket.

answer.text: Exactly one entry, with overflow probed into the next free slot

feedback.text: That describes open addressing, not chaining.

answer.text: A sorted array that is rebuilt on every insertion

feedback.text: Standard chaining uses an unsorted list; no full rebuild per insert.

answer.text: A pointer to the previous bucket in the table

feedback.text: Buckets are independent; they do not chain to each other.

generalfeedback.text: Separate chaining resolves collisions by keeping, at each slot, a secondary container (usually a linked list) of every key mapped there.

questiontext.text: With a good hash function and load factor α = n/m kept small, what is the average time for search, insert, and delete in a chained hash table?

answer.text: O(1) expected

feedback.text: Correct — the expected chain length is α, treated as a constant when α is bounded.

answer.text: O(log n)

feedback.text: No tree search is involved; chains are scanned linearly and are short on average.

answer.text: O(n) always

feedback.text: That is the worst case, not the average with a good hash.

answer.text: O(m)

feedback.text: Cost depends on chain length (~α), not the number of slots.

generalfeedback.text: The expected number of probes is proportional to the average chain length α = n/m; keeping α = O(1) gives O(1) expected operations.

questiontext.text: What input makes a chained hash table degrade to Θ(n) per operation?

answer.text: All n keys hash to the same bucket, forming one long chain

feedback.text: Correct — the operation then scans a single list of length n.

answer.text: The keys are inserted in sorted order

feedback.text: Insertion order does not matter to a hash table.

answer.text: The load factor is exactly 0.75

feedback.text: A moderate load factor still gives O(1) expected time.

answer.text: The table has more slots than items

feedback.text: That lowers α and improves performance.

generalfeedback.text: If every key collides into one bucket, the chain has length n and every operation becomes a linear list traversal.

questiontext.text: Which is a genuine advantage of separate chaining over open addressing?

answer.text: Deletion is straightforward — no tombstone markers are needed

feedback.text: Correct — you simply unlink the node from its chain.

answer.text: It stores everything in the table array with no pointer overhead

feedback.text: That is a benefit of open addressing; chaining adds pointer overhead.

answer.text: It guarantees O(1) worst-case operations

feedback.text: Chaining is O(1) only on average; a bad hash gives O(n).

answer.text: It has better cache locality than a contiguous array

feedback.text: Scattered list nodes usually have worse locality than open addressing.

generalfeedback.text: Chaining deletes in O(1) by unlinking and needs no tombstones, but pays in pointer memory and poorer cache locality.

questiontext.text: In separate chaining the load factor α = n/m may exceed 1, because chains can keep growing and the table never "fills up".

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — there is no fixed capacity; a bucket's chain simply lengthens.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Unlike open addressing, chaining has no hard ceiling on α.

questiontext.text: Separate chaining needs no extra memory beyond the table array itself.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Each list node carries at least one extra pointer, adding overhead.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — pointers (and node allocations) impose extra memory cost.

questiontext.text: Storing all keys that map to the same slot together in a linked list is the collision-resolution strategy called separate ______.

answer.text: chaining

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: chaining*

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: chain

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about separate chaining are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Deletion is simple: just unlink the node from its chain

feedback.text: Yes — no tombstones are required, unlike open addressing.

answer.text: The load factor α can be greater than 1

feedback.text: Yes — chains grow without a fixed capacity limit.

answer.text: All entries are stored directly inside the table array with no external nodes

feedback.text: No — that is open addressing; chaining stores entries in external list nodes.

answer.text: It guarantees O(1) worst-case time regardless of the hash function

feedback.text: No — a bad hash can pile all keys into one chain, giving O(n).

generalfeedback.text: Chaining allows easy deletion and α > 1, but stores entries in external nodes and only gives O(1) on average, not in the worst case.
